questions.title: Same-data original-format control
questions.comment: Could you report LTX-2.3 fine-tuned on the same data with prose-style prompts, to separate the contribution of the data from that of the screenplay format and the Director?
questions.intro: Compare the 8k stage-1 variants and the two 10k continuation variants.

questions.title: Quantitative annotation audit
questions.comment: Could you report the error rates of the annotation pipeline on a random sample (e.g., wrong speaker assignment), compared with Gemini-only annotation?
questions.intro: Compare binding accuracy and error rates.

questions.title: Component choices and methodological contribution
questions.comment: W1: the paper lacks elegance that might be desired on such a project. The system involves countless different pre-trained all knotted together (I count: Qwen, Gemma, Gemini, Keye, LTX) across textual, auditory and visual modalities. The authors neither provide quantitative evidence for each choice nor in my judgement make any attempt to brings things together in a more coherent way. It's somehow unsurprising that if one adds in all these pre-trained models, better performance is achievable. Beyond the screenplay curation, I don't think the conditioned video generation training is particularly novel.
questions.intro: Compare the WER of final annotations with different ASR priors.

questions.title: Skipped ratings
questions.comment: Q1: How often did the human raters skip? Is this making differences look bigger than they are?
questions.intro: View valid ratings and skips for each criterion.

questions.title: Data provenance and public access
questions.comment: Q2: training data is listed as publicly downloadable with added internal data. Both concern me as e.g. MovieNet video is not public and not sharing internal data or detailing is an issue for reproducibility. Do you have any comments?
questions.intro: Open the source links in the tables.

questions.title: Character binding beyond frontal faces
questions.comment: How robust is the model's character binding capability? Specifically, what level of improvement can be achieved for non-human characters, characters that are partially off-screen or occluded, or characters lacking a frontal face (e.g., those shown only in profile)?
questions.intro: View the overall accuracy, then compare the requested character in each video pair.

questions.title: Script edits and complex scenes
questions.comment: Can the model's script execution capability be further verified? For instance, in edge cases where the speaker of a specific line, the executor of an action, or the chronological order of two events is altered, does the generated output change accordingly? Furthermore, can the model handle more complex scenarios, such as martial arts scenes or scenes with a larger number of characters?
questions.intro: Compare speaker assignment and event order. Additional clips show larger casts and martial arts.

questions.title: Benchmark composition and category results
questions.comment: While Director-Bench claims coverage of multi-language, multi-character, and non-human scenarios, it does not report the sample size, number of dialogue turns, or complexity distribution for each category. Since the automatic binding metric is only applicable to 31 cases featuring frontal human faces, the overall results likely reflect this specific subset. I recommend providing a detailed breakdown of the benchmark's composition and stratified results for key categories to clarify the scope of the generalization claims. For categories with very few samples, reporting case-by-case results would suffice, without the need for new large-scale evaluations.
questions.intro: View the benchmark composition and category ratings.

questions.title: Action logic and spatial execution
questions.comment: I am curious whether the introduction of this structured script improves the logical coherence of actions or the spatial consistency in the generated videos.
questions.intro: Compare gesture timing, which character stays in view, and corridor reverberation.

questions.title: Training budget
questions.comment: What are the specific number of training steps and the computational cost (e.g., GPU hours) for the two training stages?
questions.intro: View the update counts and estimated training cost.

groups.title: An exchange in the ice cave
groups.description: Watch which character exits: the orange puppet should leave; the blue puppet should remain.

videos.label: Ours
videos.prompt:
Structured Description:
    [SCENE]
        dimly lit icy cave; blue ice formations, snow; medium close-up
    [END_SCENE]
    [VISIBLE_MAIN_CHARACTER]
        <count>3</count>
        <first>
            <appearance>orange puppet with purple hair, purple scarf, yellow-purple striped sleeves, backpack</appearance>
            <posture>standing upright</posture>
            <frame_position>frame-left</frame_position>
            <actions>faces right, looking at the blue puppet</actions>
        </first>
        <second>
            <appearance>green puppet with yellow hair, red earmuffs, green sweater</appearance>
            <posture>standing upright</posture>
            <frame_position>frame-center</frame_position>
            <actions>faces right, looking at the blue puppet</actions>
        </second>
        <third>
            <appearance>blue puppet with light blue hair, tunic with ruffled edges</appearance>
            <posture>standing upright</posture>
            <frame_position>frame-right</frame_position>
            <actions>turns head left and right, speaking to the other puppets</actions>
        </third>
    [END_VISIBLE_MAIN_CHARACTER]
    [EVENT_SEQUENCE]
        <first>
            <dialogue>
                <voice>adult female, slightly annoyed and questioning</voice>
                <character_id>speaker_1: orange puppet with purple hair</character_id>
                <words: English>Hey, how come you didn't wait for me?</words>
            </dialogue>
            <event>speaker_1 speaks while looking at speaker_3</event>
            <lighting>cool blue ambient light with soft shadows</lighting>
            <camera_motion>The camera holds a static shot on the three puppets.</camera_motion>
        </first>
        <second>
            <dialogue>
                <voice>adult male, raspy and dismissive</voice>
                <character_id>speaker_3: blue puppet with light blue hair</character_id>
                <words: English>Well, if you're gonna walk slow, don't walk when I see Joe.</words>
            </dialogue>
            <event>speaker_3 turns his head to speak to speaker_1 and speaker_2</event>
            <lighting>unchanged cool blue lighting</lighting>
            <camera_motion>The camera holds a static shot.</camera_motion>
        </second>
        <third>
            <dialogue>
                <voice>adult male, raspy and excited</voice>
                <character_id>speaker_3: blue puppet with light blue hair</character_id>
                <words: English>Oh, I like that, Flomo.</words>
            </dialogue>
            <event>speaker_3 turns forward and speaks excitedly as speaker_1 exits frame-left</event>
            <lighting>unchanged cool blue lighting</lighting>
            <camera_motion>The camera holds a static shot.</camera_motion>
        </third>
    [END_EVENT_SEQUENCE]
    [AUDIO_CAPTION]
        raspy male and clear female puppet voices, soft cave ambience
    [END_AUDIO_CAPTION]
    [SUBJECT]["people", "indoor", "other"][END_SUBJECT]
    [ATMOSPHERE]"playful, whimsical, fantasy"[END_ATMOSPHERE]

videos.label: LTX-2.3
videos.prompt: A medium close-up in a dimly lit icy cave frames three upright puppets against blue ice formations and snow, with the orange puppet with purple hair, a purple scarf, yellow-and-purple striped sleeves, and a backpack standing frame-left facing right; the green puppet with yellow hair, red earmuffs, and a green sweater standing frame-center facing right; and the blue puppet with light blue hair and a ruffled tunic standing frame-right, turning his head left and right. The camera holds a static shot on the three puppets under cool blue ambient light with soft shadows. The orange puppet, in a slightly annoyed, questioning adult female voice, says, "Hey, how come you didn't wait for me?" The blue puppet, in a raspy, dismissive adult male voice, replies, "Well, if you're gonna walk slow, don't walk when I see Joe." Then, turning forward excitedly as the orange puppet exits frame-left, he adds in a raspy, excited adult male voice, "Oh, I like that, Flomo." Raspy male and clear female puppet voices sit over soft cave ambience, keeping the scene playful, whimsical, and fantastical.

A loud, off-screen male voice then shouts, "Open up," while muffled background shouting continues. The camera remains static throughout, holding the man in sharp focus. The lighting stays dim with a warm background glow, casting a tense, cinematic atmosphere.
